# Conti Ransomware: Leaks, Ransomware-as-a-Service Structure, and Public Attribution Records

## Executive Summary

The available public record describes Conti as a large, commercially organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation rather than a small, informal criminal collective. Public reporting portrays the group as operating through specialized personnel, affiliates, initial-access brokers, technical developers, negotiators, and administrative functions. Its business model relied on obtaining access to victim environments, deploying ransomware, stealing and encrypting data, and using the threat of publication to pressure victims into paying. The evidence also indicates that Conti was associated with other malware and intrusion tools, including TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The February–March 2022 ContiLeaks disclosures exposed internal communications that made this commercialization unusually visible. Rapid7 reports that the leaked material included approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs distributed across 393 JSON files, alongside screenshots, discussions of tools and exploits, operational information, and alleged credentials. The leaks depicted hiring, salary negotiations, product development, testing against security software, phishing operations, and infrastructure management. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The law-enforcement and government attribution record is more precise about organizational and operational associations than about individual identity. The U.S. Rewards for Justice program identifies the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti and Wizard Spider. It offers up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of qualifying actors involved in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure while acting at the direction or control of a foreign government. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

Separately, a U.S. Department of Justice case page identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko as defendants in Conti-related prosecutions. The page states that the first four were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, while Lytvynenko was charged in connection with a conspiracy to deploy Conti and later pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The supplied records do not establish that any of these defendants is identical to one of the five aliases listed by Rewards for Justice. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

My assessment is that the evidence strongly supports describing Conti as a scalable, structured RaaS enterprise with a substantial operational footprint and a documented connection to Russian-linked cyber activity. However, the provided sources do not support collapsing every alias, leak username, named defendant, or associated malware family into a single unified identity. Those relationships should remain qualified unless a source explicitly establishes them.

## Source Assessment and Method

This report uses four distinct source records supplied in the benchmark material:

| Source ID | Source | Principal evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Rewards for Justice, “Conti” | U.S. government description of Conti, aliases, associated tools, Russian location, reward offer, and alleged critical-infrastructure activity |
| S2 | Rapid7, “Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict” | Technical and operational analysis of the 2022 leaks and reported contents of the internal chats |
| S3 | Center for Internet Security, “The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization” | Analysis of Conti’s organizational structure, RaaS model, staffing, and commercialization |
| S4 | U.S. Department of Justice, Middle District of Tennessee, “Conti Ransomware” | Law-enforcement case information, defendants, charges, plea information, and victim figures |

The sources differ in purpose. S1 and S4 are official U.S. government records and therefore carry the greatest weight for government attribution, reward language, charges, and procedural status. S2 and S3 are cybersecurity analyses of leaked information and should be read as reporting and assessment rather than as judicial findings. Allegations are identified as such, and defendants are presumed innocent where the DOJ page expressly states that presumption.

## How Public Sources Describe Conti as an RaaS Operation

### Operating model

Rewards for Justice describes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as a Russian government-linked RaaS group that targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. The description states that Conti ransomware was first detected in 2019 and was used in more than 1,000 ransomware operations against U.S. and international critical infrastructure. The same source identifies more than 400 victimized organizations worldwide, including more than 290 in the United States. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The numerical distinction is important. “More than 1,000 ransomware operations” describes reported activity, while “more than 400 organizations worldwide” describes organizations identified as victims in the same government description. These figures should not be treated as interchangeable counts of incidents, victims, or defendants.

The DOJ’s Middle District of Tennessee page provides a separate figure, stating that Conti affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) The figures differ because the sources may use different counting methods, time periods, or definitions of “victims,” “operations,” and “organizations.” The supplied evidence does not resolve the discrepancy.

### Double-extortion practices

The public descriptions consistently identify a two-part extortion process. Conti operators typically stole victims’ files and encrypted servers and workstations. Victims were directed to contact the operators through an online portal to negotiate or complete payment. If payment was not made, the stolen information could be sold or published on a site controlled by the operators. Rewards for Justice states that some ransom demands reached as high as $25 million. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

CIS characterizes this as double extortion: the victim faces both loss of access caused by encryption and exposure of confidential information through threatened publication. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

### Division of labor and affiliate economics

CIS describes RaaS as a model in which developers lease or provide ransomware capabilities to affiliates, who conduct intrusions and share proceeds with the developers. The article gives an often-used 70–30 division as an example of profit sharing, but it does not establish that every Conti transaction used exactly that split. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The RaaS arrangement separates malware development from victim intrusion and deployment. According to the CIS analysis, initial-access brokers could sell already established access to victim environments. Affiliates could then use that access to conduct attacks, allowing the central operation to scale without performing every intrusion itself. This arrangement also distributed operational risk and enabled the core developers to focus on improving malware and infrastructure. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The evidence therefore supports a concrete characterization: Conti’s RaaS model functioned as an ecosystem involving at least a central development and coordination capability, affiliates or operators conducting intrusions, and third parties supplying access or supporting services. It does not establish that every person who used Conti malware was a formal employee or that every incident was controlled directly by a central command.

## What the Leaks Exposed About Conti’s Internal Structure

### Scale and content of the disclosures

Rapid7 reports that, on February 27, 2022, the account known as “@ContiLeaks” released a large archive of internal chat logs following Conti’s public support for the Russian government after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The initial archive reportedly contained 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. Some messages were encrypted and unavailable, making the disclosure incomplete. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The material reportedly included internal communications, screenshots of tools, discussions of exploits and design processes, usernames and passwords, alleged infrastructure access details, and a purported ransomware source-code file. Rapid7 states that it did not access remote servers using the exposed credentials and recommended against doing so. This distinction matters: the source reports what was published or alleged by the leaker, not necessarily what was independently verified. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Corporate-style functions

CIS reports that the leaks revealed distinct operational roles, including “Coders,” “Testers,” “Administrators,” “Reverse Engineers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers.” Spamming functions were reportedly contracted outside the organization. The source says that each department had its own budget, while departments could borrow funds from one another. It also reports that an insider claimed the group employed more than 60 people, mostly coders and testers, in July 2021. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

These details are significant because they demonstrate specialization. The operation did not merely acquire or distribute a static ransomware program. It reportedly maintained personnel responsible for coding, reverse engineering, testing, administration, and offensive operations. The structure resembles a technology enterprise in its allocation of labor and budgets, although the activity was criminal rather than legitimate.

### Product development and testing

Rapid7 reports that Conti’s internal discussions included difficulties encrypting very large files and efforts to develop features for particular targets. The group allegedly sought demonstrations of endpoint-detection products so that it could modify malware to evade detection. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

CIS adds that the group allocated approximately $60,000 for a valid Cobalt Strike license and spent several thousand dollars per month on security and antivirus software for testing. It also reports that reverse engineers redirected attention toward Windows 11 in July 2021. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

Taken together, these accounts support the conclusion that Conti invested in testing, compatibility, evasion, and tooling. They also help explain why the organization could operate at scale: development and operational functions were treated as continuing business processes rather than one-off criminal activity.

### Phishing and operational logistics

Rapid7 reports that phishing was a common initial-access method because it was relatively inexpensive and effective. The leaked material included phishing templates designed around payment, invoice, contract, order, and shipment themes. The same article describes discussions about malicious documents, third-party providers, and delivery methods intended to avoid detection by dynamic analysis. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The existence of phishing templates in the published material is evidence of operational preparation, not proof that every template was used successfully or against a particular named victim. The sources do not provide a complete victim-by-victim mapping of those templates.

## Public Attribution and Law-Enforcement Records

### Government attribution of aliases

Rewards for Justice identifies five online aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. It lists Russia as an associated location and identifies Conti and Wizard Spider as associated cyberthreat organizations. The page also associates Conti with Conti RaaS, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The wording is qualified. The page says the actors are “believed to be linked” to Conti; it does not, in the supplied text, provide legal names, photographs, technical indicators, or a separate identity resolution for each alias. It also does not say that all five aliases belong to one person or that every associated application was operated by each alias.

The reward is up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of any person who, while acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government, participates in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. This is a reward-program standard, not a judicial finding that each listed alias has satisfied that legal standard. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

### Criminal defendants and procedural status

The DOJ page identifies two cases. Case 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. Case 3:23-CR-00088 names Oleksii Lytvynenko. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

The page states that Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, and Zhuykov were charged in September 2023 with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. It states that Lytvynenko was charged in November 2025 with conspiracy to deploy Conti, a ransomware variant that infected computers and networks and encrypted data. The page further reports that Lytvynenko entered a guilty plea on June 10, 2026, to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

The DOJ page schedules Lytvynenko’s sentencing for September 10, 2026, and states that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. Because the assumed current date is October 1, 2026, the supplied page’s future-facing event information should not be interpreted as evidence of the sentencing outcome; no sentencing result is included in the supplied material. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

### Limits of the alias-to-defendant link

The strongest defensible conclusion is that the records establish two parallel attribution tracks:

1. **Alias and organizational attribution:** Rewards for Justice publicly links the five aliases to Conti with qualified language.
2. **Named-person prosecution:** DOJ publicly identifies five defendants in Conti-related cases and specifies charges or plea information.

The supplied records do not explicitly connect “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis” to Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, Zhuykov, or Lytvynenko. It would therefore be unsupported to state that a particular defendant used a particular alias. Nor do the sources establish that the five defendants collectively represent all of Conti’s leadership, developers, affiliates, or operators.

## Contradictions, Tensions, and Uncertainty

### Victim and operation counts

Rewards for Justice reports more than 1,000 ransomware operations and more than 400 organizations worldwide, including more than 290 in the United States. DOJ reports more than 900 affected victims worldwide. These figures are not necessarily irreconcilable because “operations,” “organizations,” and “victims” may represent different units of measurement. Nevertheless, the sources do not provide a common methodology, so the exact overall victim count remains uncertain.

### Russian government links

Rewards for Justice characterizes Conti as Russian government-linked and describes a post-invasion pledge of support to the Russian government. Rapid7 reports that a leaked conversation indicated possible FSB involvement in part of Conti’s funding and interest in files relating to Bellingcat and Alexei Navalny. Rapid7 presents this as an indication from the chats, not as a proven judicial fact. The supplied evidence therefore supports reporting a government-link assessment and an alleged leak-based indication, but not a definitive conclusion about the full nature or extent of state control. ([Rewards for Justice, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Continuity after the leaks

Rapid7 states that Conti took down exposed infrastructure after the disclosures, but that its threat-intelligence team observed a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022. CIS states that the broader Conti platform later shut down and rebranded into smaller units, with leak and negotiation infrastructure shutting down approximately a month afterward. These statements can both be true if “resumption of normal operations” refers to activity shortly after the leaks and “shutdown” refers to the later dissolution of the larger platform. The sources do not establish a single, precise date on which every Conti-associated actor ceased operating. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

## Findings

### Finding 1: Was Conti publicly described as an RaaS operation?

Yes. Official and cybersecurity sources describe Conti as a RaaS group in which specialized developers and operators supported affiliates or other participants who conducted intrusions and ransomware deployments. The operation used double extortion and associated tools and malware families.  
**Supporting entities:** Conti; Wizard Spider; RaaS; affiliates; initial-access brokers; Conti ransomware; TrickBot; IcedID; Cobalt Strike; ZLoader.  
**Sources:** S1, S3.

### Finding 2: What did the leaks reveal?

The leaks exposed internal chats, staffing practices, technical development, security testing, phishing templates, financial discussions, and alleged infrastructure information. They portrayed Conti as a structured and commercially managed criminal enterprise with specialized departments and continuing product-development processes.  
**Supporting entities:** ContiLeaks; coders; testers; administrators; reverse engineers; penetration testers/hackers; phishing; Cobalt Strike; endpoint security testing.  
**Sources:** S2, S3.

### Finding 3: What aliases are publicly linked to Conti?

Rewards for Justice identifies “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” as aliases of malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. The source does not provide a supplied alias-to-real-name mapping.  
**Supporting entities:** “Target”; “Reshaev”; “Professor”; “Tramp”; “Dandis”; Conti; Wizard Spider.  
**Sources:** S1.

### Finding 4: What named defendants are linked to Conti prosecutions?

The DOJ identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko in Conti-related cases. The supplied page reports charges against the first four and a later guilty plea by Lytvynenko to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.  
**Supporting entities:** Maksim Galochkin; Maksim Rudenskiy; Mikhail Tsarev; Andrey Zhuykov; Oleksii Lytvynenko; Conti ransomware.  
**Sources:** S4.

### Finding 5: Are the aliases and defendants explicitly matched?

No. The supplied sources establish both alias-level attribution and defendant-level prosecution, but they do not explicitly identify which, if any, defendant used any particular alias.  
**Supporting entities:** Conti aliases; DOJ defendants; Rewards for Justice; U.S. Department of Justice.  
**Sources:** S1, S4.

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a concrete and qualified conclusion: Conti was publicly characterized as a highly organized RaaS enterprise whose criminal activity was enabled by specialization, affiliate relationships, external access providers, technical development, and double-extortion practices. The ContiLeaks disclosures materially strengthened that characterization by exposing internal administrative and technical processes that resembled a commercial software organization. The leaks also showed the operational risks of political alignment and internal disagreement, although the supplied sources do not establish the complete cause-and-effect relationship between the Ukraine-related dispute, the disclosures, and the later fragmentation of the organization.

The public attribution record is substantial but should not be overstated. Rewards for Justice supplies a government assessment connecting five aliases to Conti and Wizard Spider, while the DOJ supplies named defendants and case outcomes in Conti-related prosecutions. Those records collectively establish a strong public association between Conti activity, the listed aliases, and the listed defendants at the organizational or case level. They do not, on the supplied evidence, establish direct identity matches between the aliases and defendants, nor do they prove that every associated malware tool or every reported Conti operation was controlled by the same individuals.

Malicious cyber actors known by their online aliases of “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group. Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. After Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to carry out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. First detected in 2019, Conti ransomware has been used to conduct more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure, such as law enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities. These healthcare and first responder networks are among the more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, over 290 of which are located in the United States. Conti operators typically steal victims’ files and encrypt the servers and workstations in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim. The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction. If the ransom is not paid, the stolen data is sold or published to a public site controlled by the Conti actors. Ransom amounts vary widely, with some ransom demands being as high as $25 million. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. For further discussion on how to protect yourself from ransomware, see our ransomware prevention solution . Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward. Malicious cyber actors known by their online aliases of “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group. Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. After Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to carry out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. First detected in 2019, Conti ransomware has been used to conduct more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure, such as law enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities. These healthcare and first responder networks are among the more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, over 290 of which are located in the United States. Conti operators typically steal victims’ files and encrypt the servers and workstations in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim. The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction. If the ransom is not paid, the stolen data is sold or published to a public site controlled by the Conti actors. Ransom amounts vary widely, with some ransom demands being as high as $25 million. At that time, we assessed that due to their sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021, they remained an active and significant threat. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. CIS SecureSuite® Membership Multi-State ISAC (MS-ISAC®) CIS CyberMarket® Vendors CIS Communities Our Partners Careers Home Insights Blog Posts The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization This past year saw substantial growth in ransomware incidents. Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward.
